html:
The turkey is one of the few farm animals first tamed in the Americas. People in Mesoamerica raised the wild turkey at least 2,000 years ago, and recent research suggests the Ancestral Puebloans of the American Southwest may have tamed it a second time, separately.

Turkeys were kept for meat and for their feathers, which were used in cloaks, fans and rituals. Alongside the dog, the llama and the guinea pig, they were among the very few animals the peoples of the Americas domesticated. That shortage of large farm animals is one reason American societies did not develop the same animal-borne diseases as the Old World, which made them so vulnerable after 1492.

After the Spanish conquest, the turkey crossed the Atlantic as part of the Columbian Exchange and spread quickly through Europe in the 1500s. English speakers named it after Turkey by confusion with other birds brought by Ottoman traders.
